title: Beads and hands
hookLine: the mala counts recitations on a garland of beads, often 108; mudras are the hand shapes on every Buddha statue

lines: THE SAME BEADS IN A SHOP WINDOW.
cards: A string of wooden beads on a grandmother's wrist, clicking softly through her fingers while the news plays. The same beads, in a shop window, sold as a yoga bracelet.
And on every Buddha statue you've ever passed, the hands are doing something: resting in the lap, touching the ground, raised with the palm out. None of it is random.
The beads count something, and the hands are saying something. We've spent a week on the feet. Today, the hands.

teach.h: MALA — A GARLAND YOU COUNT ON.
teach.b: The beads are a mala. You've heard the word before: Angulimala, the finger garland. Mala means garland.
A full Buddhist mala often has a hundred and eight beads, and traditions explain the number in different ways. What it's for is simple.
Each bead marks one recitation, so the fingers keep count and the mind can stay with the words. In Tibetan communities that's often a mantra.
In Japanese Pure Land temples, people hold their beads while saying the name of Amida Buddha. In parts of Southeast Asia, some count the qualities of the Buddha.
A Chinese sutra tells of a king, worn down by war and sickness, who asks the Buddha for something simple.
String a hundred and eight seeds, the Buddha tells him, and pass one through your fingers each time you recall the three jewels.
If it reminds you of a rosary, that's fair: Hindus, Catholics and Muslims count prayers on beads too. Fingers are good at keeping count.

teach.h: MUDRA — A SEAL MADE WITH THE HANDS.
teach.b: Now the hands on the statues. They're called mudras, which means seals or signs. Hands resting in the lap, right on left, thumbs lightly touching: meditation.

teach.h: REST, WITNESS, DO NOT FEAR, TEACH.
teach.b: The right hand reaching down to the ground: the earth as witness, which you met on the night of the awakening.

The right hand raised, palm out: do not fear. Thumb and finger making a circle at the chest: turning the wheel of the teaching. Once you know them, a statue tells you which moment of the story it's showing.

how: Many Buddhists use a mala to count mantras, the Buddha's name or the three jewels, and sit with their hands in the meditation mudra, resting in the lap with the thumbs lightly touching.

games.q: you're a king worn down by war and sickness, with no time for long practice. you ask the Buddha for something simple. in the Chinese sutra, what does he give you?
o: a year of retreat in the forest.
108 seeds on a string, one for each recollection.
games.why: a string of seeds, passed through the fingers each time he recalls the Buddha, the teaching and the community.

practice: Sit, and rest your hands in your lap, right hand on left, palms up, thumbs lightly touching. Many Zen teachers say the thumbs are a quiet signal: pressing hard means tension, drifting apart means drowsiness.
Now count the breath on your fingers, or on a mala if you have one: one breath, one finger or one bead. When you lose count, begin again at one.

wordCard.voice: Mala. A garland: a string of beads, often a hundred and eight, that counts recitations. The same word as in Angulimala. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: garland. The hand signs are mudra, मुद्रा (MOO-draa), a seal.

carryVoice: Your line: the hands remember. A bead or a resting hand can hold your place when the mind wanders off. Day one hundred twenty-two.
